A bargain is fundamentally about two people reaching an agreement — usually an agreement where each person gives something and gets something in return. Think of it as a settled deal between two sides, where both have agreed on the terms.

But the word also has a second, very common meaning: something you get at a price lower than it is normally worth — a surprisingly good deal for the buyer.

Both meanings are standard and widely used in English. Context tells you which one is meant.

In this sense, a bargain is an arrangement two parties have negotiated and accepted. Each side agrees to do (or give) something, and in return, the other side agrees to do (or give) something back.

The two companies made a bargain: one would supply the raw materials, and the other would handle the shipping.

Key features of a bargain in this sense:

  • There are two or more parties involved.
  • There has been some negotiation — the terms weren't simply imposed by one side.
  • Both sides have accepted the terms. A bargain is complete only once agreement is reached.
  • It creates a kind of mutual obligation — each party is expected to hold up their end.

This type of bargain can be formal (like a legal contract) or informal (like a simple spoken agreement between friends). What matters is that both sides have willingly agreed.

They struck a bargain: he would teach her to drive, and she would help him with his essays.

The phrase "strike a bargain" or "make a bargain" means to successfully reach and agree on such a deal.
Meaning 2 — Something Bought at a Lower Price Than Expected

This is the everyday shopping sense of the word. When you buy something and the price is much lower than what it is normally sold for — or lower than what it is truly worth — that item is called a bargain.

I found a beautiful leather jacket at the market for only ₹500. It was a real bargain.

In this sense, the word always carries a positive feeling for the buyer. The buyer feels they got more value than they paid for. The word implies:

  • The price was lower than usual or expected.
  • The quality is good relative to the price.
  • There is a sense of satisfaction or good fortune on the buyer's part.

You'll often see or hear phrases like:

  • "What a bargain!" — expressing pleasant surprise at a low price.
  • "That's a bargain." — confirming that the price is impressively low.
  • "Bargain prices" — used in advertisements to suggest very low prices.
  • "Bargain hunter" — a person who actively seeks out low-priced goods.
The Connection Between the Two Meanings

The two meanings are not entirely separate in spirit. In the first meaning, a bargain is an agreement where both sides feel the exchange is fair or worthwhile. In the second meaning, a bargain is a purchase where the buyer feels the deal is in their favour. Both ideas share the underlying sense of a deal that feels worth it.

A "good bargain" vs. a "bad bargain"
These phrases apply to Meaning 1. A good bargain is an agreement where you got favorable terms — you came out ahead or at least fairly. A bad bargain is one where, in hindsight, you agreed to terms that were not in your favour.

In the end, he realized he had made a bad bargain — he gave up too much.

"Drive a hard bargain"
This phrase is important. If someone drives a hard bargain, it means they negotiate very firmly and push very strongly for the best possible terms for themselves. It's often said with a hint of respect for their toughness in negotiations, though it can also carry a suggestion that they were difficult to deal with.

She drives a hard bargain — we ended up agreeing to all her conditions.

"Into the bargain"
This is a fixed phrase meaning "in addition to everything else" or "as an extra." It's used to mention something that comes on top of what was already being discussed — often something surprising or noteworthy.

The apartment was spacious and affordable — and it came with a parking space into the bargain.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Deal — very close in meaning to bargain (both meanings), but "deal" is a broader, more casual word. Every bargain can be called a deal, but not every deal carries the sense of negotiation that "bargain" implies.
  • Agreement — more neutral and formal. An agreement may not involve any back-and-forth negotiation at all. A bargain specifically implies that terms were discussed and settled.
  • Contract — a formal, legally binding agreement. A bargain can be informal; a contract cannot.
  • Discount — refers only to a reduction in price, not to the item itself. A discount is the reduction; the item you buy because of that discount might be called a bargain.

A bargain is either (1) a mutual agreement reached through negotiation, where both parties agree to give and receive something — or (2) an item or purchase that costs less than its usual or expected price, making the buyer feel they've gotten exceptional value. Both uses share the spirit of a deal that feels worthwhile.
